18.t: Editorial
The ’68-69 school year has witnessed a number of changes. Towering above all
was of course the change of the Principal. Rev. Fr. Foley, our former Principal and
Rector, has joined the teaching staff of Wan Yan College, Kowloon, and we wish him
success in teaching in the years to come. In his stead is Rev. Fr. Deignan, the former
Prefect of Studies. With years of administrative experience, he is more than capable of
being our new Headmaster. Mr. P. L. Yu is now our Assistant Principal with Mr. S. H.
Chau as Deputy Assistant Principal.
Both have acquired invaluable teaching experience
before assuming their respective positions.
We also welcomed to the teaching staff Fr. M. Brosnan （F5），Mr. C. Y. Chan
（Biology）， Miss H. Ho （Eng. & Hist.） and Mrs. Yung （Music）； while Fr. R. McCarthy and
Fr. P. Reynolds went on study leaves and Mr. Philip Tsoi, who was with us for 6 years，
left for Queen's College. We welcomed back, after 5 years' absence in Kowloon, Fr. M.
Corbally who is now Rector as well as Form-master of his old 4D again.
On 6th May, one of our students, Ho Wai Luen （3D） died in hospital after being
seriously injured in an accident at lunch-time the previous day near the school entrance.
His classmates and teachers attended his funeral two days later. To his parents and family
we offer our deepest sympathy.
Shortly after the start of the school year, Fr. Deignan introduced assembly meetings
for junior and senior boys regularly once every two weeks, during which school events
were announced. This enabled many students who hitherto were unconscious of anything
but their studies, to become aware of the extracurricular activities. Its success was clearly
manifested by the general improvement in public-spirit shown by the students. Assembly
is here to stay for it is recognised that it is beneficial to the running of the school.
Up to now, the publication of the STAR has been a headache for the Father-editor
only. This eaition, however, is different from its predecessors: the students have shoulder-
ed the burden.“Burden' sounds a bit forbidding, but the students are wiling to take up
the responsioility.
The Student Council this year has certainly done a good job. It is to be credited
With organizing such events as the Teachers' Day and the Annual Drama Competition, of
which the former was an unprecedented event.
The Fathers and ieachers were satisfied，
and so was the Council itself.

19.t: ‘Studies should go hand in hand with extracurricular activities'， so the saying goes.
In this respect, Wah Yan does not lag behind. Several new clubs, viz. the Mathematics
Club, the Social Activities Club and the Tennis Club, were established, while the scholas-
Thanks are due to our Principal for his Kind advice, to our advertisers without whom
the production of the STAR would be impossible, to the Editorial Board for the precious
time they have sacrificed, to our photographers and Mainland Studio, and to our printer.
It goes without saying that the time spent in school is the most memorable in our short
span of years. This book is of course dedicated to all W.Y. students, but especially to
those who have left. The STAR brings them reminiscences of their happy school life in
•Good Old Wah Yan'， so that they can recapture the joy of innocence and mischief in
junior forms, and achievement and pride in higher forms.
Those who are leaving this year
can on the one hand picture in their minds the great and challenging time ahead of them，
and on the other recall the atmosphere of friendliness that existed for them, and always
exists, in Wah Yan. To have done this is to have the purpose of the STAR well served.

OBITUARY
Mr Patrick
Cromwell Hall
THE LATE PATRICK CROMWELL HALL
（Dred 25 January 1969）
Patrick Cromwell Hall, who died in January, was always a very loyal and generous
Past Student of Wah Yan College with which he kept close contact ever since graduating
in July 1939 after completing his secondary school course. He was born in Hong Kong
on 14th September 1924 and entered the College in September 1933. In 1945 he took up
the pharmaceutical business and started the Kowloon Dispensary soon afterwards. He be-
came the sole proprietor of the firm in 1963.
Patrick was very active in many fields, notably social work. He was a member and
also held office in a number of professional medical and pharmaceutical associations; Hon.
Ireasurer of the Tsim Sha Tsui Kai-Fong Welfare Association; Past Hon. Treasurer, Kow-
loon Rotary Club; member of the HK Road Safety Assoc.， the Kowloon Chamber of Com-
merce, the Chinese Catholic Club, the HK Civic Assoc. Patrick was also on the Executive
Committee of the Jesuit Graduates International Assoc.， a President and later Hon. President
of the Wah Yan Past Students' Association, and, at the time of his death, Vice-Chairman of
the Wah Yan Past Students’Association, Kowloon.
To his bereaved wife, sons and daughter, we offer our deepest condolences.

In Memory of a Late Classmate 一
It was a hot, cloudless afternoon in
Everyone in our class was busily
answering Chinese History questions when
our form-master, Mr. Cheng, came in
and gave us a piece of shocking news. Our
class-prefect, Ho Wai Luen, had been
knocked down by a car and was now in a
very serious condition in the hospital, he
told us. The rest of that day passed with
each of us feeling very uneasy.
The next day, the bad news came
our friend had passed away. I was shock-
ea and could hardly speak.
Wal Luen was a tall, thin, young boy
wno wore a pair Of spectacles. He was a
silent person and seldom spoke to others
first, but he was very friendly towaras his
classmates and always did his best to help
them.
As the Class prefect, he always
carried out his duties faithfully without
complaints. Both the teachers and his class-
mates liked him very much.
Although he was not very good at his
studies, he was always trying his very best
to improve. I always saw him study during
the lunch-break and recesses while the
others were playing in the play-ground. So
lam sure that he would have been success-
ful in the final examination if he had not
been killed.
I am very sorry for his sudden death
and miss him very much. Although he
cannot be seen any more, I will remember
him forever and I hope he is now enjoying
everlasting peace and happiness in heaven.
Li Shu Chuen （F3D）

Introduction
Silvermine Bay is on the NE of Lantao
The whole area was affected by
submergence once, but now, the alluvium
brought down by the streams has filled
up the area, forming an infilled valley.
Rock type of the area varies from place to
place, but granite and granite porphyry are
the main constituents.
The latter often
appears in the form of dykes. Syenite （an
igneous rock without quartz） can be found
just south of the sandspit, west of the pier.
General Description
The beach of Silvermine Bay is mark-
ed oy a sanaspit, nearly linked up at the
free end with the coast. It is caused by a
longshore drift from the north. Here, the
tetcn Is over 20 miles and so the drift is
quite a strong one. The materials making
up the spit may be partly brought down by
the streams and partly derived from the
weathering and erosion of the coast near-by.
The sanaspit encloses a lagoon on its
west which is wide and shallow.
There are
lots of mangrove swamps and mudfiats.
The lagoon provides a haven for the fishing
junks.

which is very fertile.
Farming is practised

gradient very gentle. The streams here
are

in

105.t: RAIN
Either in slashing showers or gentle
drizzles the rain has been falling ever since
the beginning of the world. It is the
origin of many catastrophes, but it is also
one of the most important elements for
sustaining life in our world.
In our ordinary view, rain is an
irritating thing that keeps us from going
out, or makes us all wet when on our way
to school, or makes us cancel all our plans
for the day. Rain can surely be irritating，
especlally that which talls wnen you are
out without being prepared for it. Such an
experience can happen to anyone, and the
Victims, all drenched to the skin, can easily
catch a cold.
outdoor, either for a walk or to the bus
stop, requires our consideration if there is
rain. There is never a possibility of having
a gooa time if heavy rain comes and keeps
you home; no football, no movies, no out-
door activities, having only to wait for the
weather to improve.
Does this irritate
you？
Furthermore, there is an impending
danger whenever rain falls heavily. Sudden
landslides and floods have taken the lives of
thousands and ruined many homes. Thou-
sands can be made homeless with their pro-
perty washed away. Landslides are just as
dangerous, as they usually occur unexpect-
edly, burying alive those unfortunate souls
who happen to pass by.
Although a great menace, rain plays an
important part in our lives. Water from
rain is used in great amounts every day.
Humans use it for washing and generating
power. Plants, biras, animals and insects
also require it for maintaining their exis-
tence. Imagine the result of having no rain；
every single blade of grass would perish，
Ieaving only a dry, barren desert behind. All
the glamour and picturesque scenes that
the rain brings to the world would be lost.
It is rain that makes flowers thrive in the
gardens, that makes our reservoirs filled to
the brim with water we need so badly, and
enables us to dwell in comfort in a world
worth living in.
So next time When you Know the rain
is about to fall remember what we owe to
it and smile joyfully to receive it.
